Linux Laptop Buyer's Guide: Tips And Resources To Find The Perfect Laptop For Your Favorite Distro

Avoid most cheap new laptops. Consumer laptops are largely junk. You can find a decent one once in a while, but all the name brands sell garbage consumer laptops at prices under $1,000. A used business model will be cheaper and last longer with less headaches. You'll also have a better understanding of how well it will support Linux by reviews or forum threads from people online.

Some random thoughts about laptops:

  • People are fucking wimps about laptop thickness, slickness, weight in grams, etc. But sane people don't really need a fully functional computer that they can use while dancing! Laptops are really portable office-in-a-backpack solutions you can carry from one location with a table to another, and set up in a minute or two. I can carry a 200lb backpack; I don't mind carrying a few extra pounds in a laptop.

  • There is no such thing as a laptop with a good keyboard. (Not even the old Thinkpad was perfect.) This is because laptops are mass produced, but 99% of people are idiots. So the best that 1% non-idiots can do is buy a separate keyboard. (And mouse/etc if you really need it, but thanks to i3 and Vimium you very rarely do.)

    • An added advantage of this is that you can plug or Bluetooth your input to different devices (desktop, laptop, tablet, phone, even watch!) without screwing your muscle memory.

    • If you're using a separate keyboard, then a "2-in-1" laptop that can stand in a "tent" position is an advantage.

  • There is no such thing as a laptop with a good internal battery for everyone's needs. How much battery you need varies drastically based on circumstance. If you live in the woods (like me), you want external battery packs that will keep all your electronics (laptops, 4G hotspot, USB-rechargable lights, etc) running for days. External batteries are far more cost-effective and flexible than ones specific to any laptop. A USB-C battery might not be enough for a more powerful laptop, but a battery with an inverter and AC outlets is an overkill (conversion from DC to AC to DC is a huge waste). A battery with a 20v DC connector is ideal.

  • There is no such thing as one perfect laptop for everything. Most of the time I like having a powerful 17" laptop with a good CPU and lots of RAM, but sometimes I want a light energy-efficient 11" tablet, or a simple dumb MP3 player. So having multiple devices is ideal.

• If you end up buying something cheap or used, take a look at how much RAM it has. You want at least 8GB nowadays, so you can open up tons of tabs, text, photos, video editors, etc. at the same time without things getting slow. If you only have 4 GB, for the love of god, upgrade.

  • Also fuck HDDs in laptops. Expect them to die any time your backpack slightly bumps something, so be sure to always make backups using rsync for files and maybe occasionally clonezilla for a system image. Get whichever laptop makes sense to you, then when the warranty expires, swap out the HDD with an SSD and reinstall Linux. The SSD is sturdier and will save you a minute or more every time you boot. Two tweaks to optimize your SSD's lifespan on Linux: To reduce writes disable journaling on ext4 or use btrfs and also activate trim.

  • If your laptop has a CD drive, you can take it out and insert a second hard drive inside a hard drive caddy that costs under $5. Then you can have an SSD for speed and HDD for cheap mass storage in the same laptop.

I would never use a laptop spinning disk drive as the main OS drive. I would grudgingly use one as a second drive for storage, but a regular spinning disk drive in an external enclosure would work much better.

Laptop spinning disk drives are slow and they get even slower over time. An SSD brings your laptop’s drive up to desktop speed. Even a cheap SSD blows away any spinning disk drive. When I switched my old laptop over to one it was like breathing new life into the machine.
